### Question 1

Watching clouds pile up in the afternoon is one thing. Saying 'we should move the picnic inside, it will pour within the hour' is a different move: you took what you can see now and ran it forward in time. That forward run is anticipatory thinking, and nurses do it with heart rates, urine output, and breathing patterns instead of clouds.

### Question 2

Three things could be making a noise on your bike: a loose bell, a slipping chain, or a cracked brake. You check the brake first, not because it is the most likely, but because that is the one that hurts you if you guess wrong. Weighing 'how likely' against 'how bad if true' is exactly what prioritizing hypotheses means.

### Question 3

A low-fuel light does not add gasoline to the tank. It is useful only because it warns you while you still have enough road to reach a station instead of stalling on the shoulder. Prediction gives nursing that same margin, which is what turns a crisis into something handled early and calmly.

### Question 4

One photograph of a car tells you where it sits. A few seconds of video tells you which way it is moving and how fast, so you can say where it will be shortly. Patient data works the same way: prediction needs the video, and a lone vital sign is only the still frame.

### Question 5

Leg muscles work like a hand squeezing a tube from the bottom, pushing venous blood up toward the heart with every step. Days of lying still means nobody is squeezing, so blood lingers in the calf veins. Blood that sits still is blood that clots, which is why clot risk is predictable, not surprising, in a patient who cannot move.

### Question 6

Before a race you name a target finishing time; afterward you hold the clock up against that target. The target has to exist first or the clock is just a number with nothing to say. Nursing works the same way when you state 'this antipyretic should bring the fever down within an hour' and then go back and check.

### Question 7

A smoke detector exists to sell you minutes. If you wait until flames reach the hallway, every one of those minutes has already been spent, and the only options left are the expensive ones. Skipping anticipatory thinking does not simplify a shift; it just guarantees that every problem arrives at its most demanding stage.

### Question 8

Picture a tank with a slow leak and a pump working to hold the level steady. As the level drops the pump runs faster, so for a while the gauge looks nearly normal even though the pump is straining. A climbing pulse paired with a sinking blood pressure is that straining pump, and it tells you the leak has not stopped.

### Question 9

A lifeguard does not jog to the equipment shed once a swimmer starts struggling; the rescue tube is already in hand before anyone enters the water. Suction set up before the first bite is the same decision. You cannot guarantee the event will not happen, but you can decide in advance how many seconds it will cost you.

### Question 10

A trained distance runner may rest at a pulse in the forties; finding that same runner at 80 is textbook-normal and also nearly double their usual, which is worth a second look. Meanwhile someone who has lived at 160/95 for years is not in crisis at that number. Reference ranges describe crowds, and prediction is about watching one person move away from their own starting point.

### Question 11

Recovery has an expected shape: soreness that eases a little each day. What raises the alarm on day three is not that the pain is severe but that it is moving the wrong direction, and the fever arriving alongside it says the same thing. You can only notice a wrong direction if you are carrying a map of the right one, which is why knowing the normal course is part of the skill.

### Question 12

Every treatment is a trade, and predicting well means naming both sides of it before the first dose. Opening the drain to let excess fluid out works, but potassium leaves in that same fluid rather than staying behind. So the nurse plans to watch two things at once: the swelling and lung sounds improving, and the potassium not sliding too far while that happens.
